newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks depressed by Bhutto killing.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks depressed by Bhutto killing.

text.p: Pakistani stocks, already depressed by a gloomy economic outlook, plunged on Sunday in reaction to the killing of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto, dealers said.
They said Murtaza's death had fuelled political uncertainty and the market would suffer as long as doubts over the future of Bhutto's nearly three-year-old government persist.
Murtaza, 42, leader of a breakaway faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party, and seven of his supporters died after a clash with police outside his Karachi home on Friday night.
"The situation was bad and it is getting worse," dealer Zaina Nosherwan of Taurus Securities said after the Karachi 100-share index dipped 23.29 points to close at 1,415.52.

She said Murtaza's shooting indicated that the police, themselves accused of using excessive force and killing people in fabricated clashes, were unlikely to be able to control the political unrest that has tormented Karachi.
Many dealers linked the killing to the government's policy of giving the police a free hand to quell militants of the Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM).
Some also expressed fear that the shooting might have been deliberately planned to destabilise the Bhutto government.
Murtaza's supporters and opposition politicians have said Benazir and her husband, Investment Minister Asif Ali Zardari, are directly or indirectly responsible for his death.
"The market will get really weak as the country seems to be heading for new heights of political uncertainty," analyst Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co said.
He said most market players would adopt a wait-and-see approach while foreign investors would certainly become more cautious about buying Pakistani stocks.
"Things will remain murky till we can make some sense out of the worsening political scenario," Sheikh said.
He said the market could shake off its blues only if the political scene stabilised and talks with the International Monetary Fund in Washington proved positive.

A delegation led by V.A. Jafarey, Bhutto's adviser on finance, is due to meet IMF officials in the next few days to try to persuade them to release delayed tranches of a $600 million standby loan due in June and September.
The IMF has held up disbursements because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed policies and confusion surrounding the budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
It can only resume payments once an IMF mission completes a review of Pakistan's economic performance to the satisfaction of the IMF board. No date has been set for such a mission.
"We don't expect positive political news, but something good from the economic front could stabilise the market," said dealer Khalid Hussain of National Investment and Finance Services.
